parole.significato: A narrow bar of sand or gravel formed by the sea; a sandbank.
parole.testo: From an unattested Norn word, from Old Norse eyrr. Compare Icelandic eyri, Norwegian øyr.

parole.significato: An inlet, gully or cleft in the face of a cliff.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norn gjo, from Old Norse gjá.

parole.significato: The highest court, which was held every summer from medieval times until around the 17th century.
parole.testo: From Norn, ultimately from Old Norse lǫg (“law”) + þing (“a legal assembly”). Doublet of Lagting.

parole.significato: Seafire, phosphorescence on the ocean, especially around the Shetland Islands.
parole.testo: From an unattested Norn term *mareld, from Old Norse mǫrueldr, from marr (“sea”) + eldr (“fire”). Compare Icelandic maurildi, Swedish mareld.
As the term was originally used in the Scottish Isles, particularly the Shetlands, it probably derives from Norn tåisti, from Old Norse þeisti. Compare with Norwegian Nynorsk teist.

Borrowed from Norn umbod, ombod, from Old Norse umboð. Cognate with Icelandic umboð, Faroese umboð, Swedish ombud. Cognate with the first element of ombudsman (equivalent to umboth + -s- + man, “person of agency”).

parole.significato: A narrow sea inlet, particularly in the Shetland Islands, similar to a fjord.
parole.testo: Shetland and Orkney dialect, from Norn, from Old Norse vágr (“inlet, bay”). Cognate with Swedish and Norwegian våg, and Faroese vágur. Doublet of way.

parole.significato: Any of a large number of species of small rodents of the tribes Arvicolini, Ellobiusini, Clethrionomyini, Pliomyini, Ph…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norn vollj, from Old Norse vǫllr (“field”), from Proto-Germanic *walþuz (“forest”). The Orkney dialectal term vole mouse, lit. “field mouse”, was introduced to general English by George Barry in 1805; John Fleming in 1828 was first to refer to the creature by the epithet vole alone.
